DA-1726: The Oxyntomodulin Analog Targeting Both Obesity and Fatty Liver Disease — Research Dossier

Medical Disclaimer: Research compounds discussed for educational purposes only. DA-1726 is an investigational compound in Phase 1 clinical trials and is not FDA-approved or approved anywhere as of November 2026. No information here constitutes medical advice. Consult a healthcare provider before any clinical decision.

What Is DA-1726?

DA-1726 is an investigational peptide drug developed by MetaVia Inc. that is engineered from the structure of oxyntomodulin (OXM) — a naturally occurring gut hormone that your small intestine already produces after meals. Unlike most obesity drugs in development, which target GLP-1 receptors and optionally GIP receptors, DA-1726 pairs GLP-1 receptor agonism with glucagon receptor agonism — a combination that creates unique advantages specifically for liver fat disease alongside obesity.

At the Precision Liver Symposium 2026 in Denver (November 6, 2026), MetaVia presented interim Phase 1 Part 3B results showing:

  • 13.5% placebo-adjusted body weight reduction
  • 68% placebo-adjusted liver fat reduction (measured by MRI-PDFF)

For a Phase 1 trial — which is typically designed to test safety, not efficacy — these metabolic signals are significant, and the liver fat number is among the strongest early-stage results seen in the emerging MASLD/MASH drug pipeline.

What Is Oxyntomodulin?

Oxyntomodulin (OXM) is a 37-amino acid peptide encoded by the same proglucagon gene that produces GLP-1 and glucagon. It's secreted from intestinal L-cells after eating and naturally engages both the GLP-1 receptor and the glucagon receptor — giving it dual metabolic activity that neither GLP-1 nor glucagon alone provides.

Academic researchers at Imperial College London demonstrated in Phase 1/2 studies in the 2000s that native oxyntomodulin reduced body weight and food intake in humans. The problem: OXM has a half-life of only a few minutes in the bloodstream, requiring multiple daily injections — impractical for clinical use. DA-1726 solves this engineering problem: MetaVia modified the OXM peptide to extend its half-life to support once-weekly subcutaneous dosing, the same administration schedule as the leading GLP-1 drugs.

Mechanism of Action: Two Receptors, Two Metabolic Pathways

GLP-1 Receptor (GLP-1R) Agonism

The foundation. GLP-1R agonism:

  • Activates hypothalamic satiety circuits — reduces appetite and food intake
  • Slows gastric emptying — prolongs the feeling of fullness
  • Stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion — improves glycemic control
  • Suppresses glucagon when blood glucose is elevated

This is the shared mechanism with semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) and all GLP-1 drugs. It's responsible for the appetite-driven component of DA-1726's weight-loss effect.

Glucagon Receptor (GCGR) Agonism

The differentiator. Glucagon receptor agonism:

  • Drives hepatic fat oxidation — directly stimulates the liver to burn stored triglycerides through beta-oxidation
  • Increases thermogenesis — raises basal metabolic rate and energy expenditure
  • Reduces hepatic steatosis — the defining pathology of MASLD (fatty liver disease)
  • Operates independently of caloric restriction — adds energy-expenditure contribution on top of appetite reduction

This is what distinguishes DA-1726 from both semaglutide (GLP-1 only) and tirzepatide (GLP-1 + GIP). Tirzepatide adds the GIP receptor for augmented incretin signaling and adipose tissue effects; DA-1726 instead adds the glucagon receptor — specifically anti-steatotic in the liver. For a drug targeting MASLD/MASH alongside obesity, that's the more mechanistically targeted choice.

Key Research Findings

Phase 1 Part 3B Interim Results (Precision Liver Symposium 2026, November 6, 2026)

MetaVia presented interim data from 19 participants (15 on DA-1726, 4 on placebo) at doses of 48 mg and 64 mg weekly:

Outcome Measure DA-1726 (Placebo-Adjusted)
Body weight reduction −13.5%
Liver fat reduction (MRI-PDFF) −68%
Uric acid reduction (mg/dL) −1.47 mg/dL (statistically significant, p<0.05)

Uric acid finding (November 12, 2026): MetaVia announced a statistically significant placebo-adjusted reduction of 1.47 mg/dL in serum uric acid from Part 3B data (n=15 on DA-1726, n=4 placebo). Uric acid elevation is a common metabolic comorbidity in MASLD, gout, and cardiovascular disease — a finding relevant to DA-1726's target patient population.

Context note: These are Phase 1 interim data from a small n=19 cohort. Phase 1 is designed to test safety/tolerability — producing these metabolic signals as secondary readouts is encouraging but requires confirmation in Phase 2/3 RCTs with larger populations.

Prior Phase 1 Data (ObesityWeek 2025)

At ObesityWeek 2025, MetaVia presented earlier Phase 1 data showing:

  • Favorable safety and tolerability profile consistent with the GLP-1/glucagon drug class
  • Pharmacokinetic (PK) profile confirming support for once-weekly dosing
  • Dose-dependent metabolic effects

Upcoming: ObesityWeek 2026 Poster (November 14, 2026)

MetaVia has an abstract accepted at ObesityWeek 2026 (Washington D.C.) for a poster titled: "DA-1726 Demonstrates Comparable Weight Loss and Distinct Metabolic Profile Compared With Retatrutide." The poster will present a comparison with retatrutide — Eli Lilly's GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist that leads all Phase 3 obesity trials. This comparison will clarify how DA-1726's dual mechanism benchmarks against the most potent obesity drug in advanced development.

Dosing in Clinical Trials

  • Administration: Once-weekly subcutaneous injection
  • Phase 1 Part 3 doses evaluated: 48 mg and 64 mg weekly
  • Dose escalation schedules used (consistent with standard incretin drug titration)
  • All Phase 1 safety data: GI-related adverse events (nausea, GI discomfort) consistent with class; no unexpected safety signals reported
  • Important: DA-1726 is investigational; doses outside of clinical trials are not approved, validated, or available

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is DA-1726 and how does it work differently from semaglutide or tirzepatide?

DA-1726 is an engineered analog of oxyntomodulin (OXM), a natural gut peptide that activates both the GLP-1 receptor and the glucagon receptor. Semaglutide activates only GLP-1R; tirzepatide activates GLP-1R and GIP receptor. DA-1726 targets GLP-1R plus glucagon receptor — the same second receptor that retatrutide uses alongside GLP-1R and GIPR. This matters because glucagon receptor agonism directly drives hepatic fat oxidation and thermogenesis — increasing energy expenditure while the GLP-1 component reduces caloric intake. For liver disease (MASLD/MASH), the glucagon receptor component is mechanistically well-matched: it removes fat from the liver through beta-oxidation, independent of caloric restriction. The 68% liver fat reduction at Phase 1 interim reflects this dual mechanism.

Q: What did the DA-1726 Phase 1 results show, and are they reliable?

At the Precision Liver Symposium 2026 (November 6, 2026), MetaVia presented interim Part 3B data from 19 participants (15 on drug, 4 on placebo): 13.5% weight loss and 68% liver fat reduction, both placebo-adjusted. These are impressive for Phase 1, but caveats apply: the sample is tiny (n=19), Phase 1 is designed for safety not efficacy, and interim results may change at topline. That said, a 68% placebo-adjusted liver fat reduction is a strong early-stage efficacy signal — placebo adjustment removes lifestyle confounding, so this represents drug-specific liver fat removal. Full topline Phase 1 data are expected Q4 2026, with Phase 2 initiation likely following.

Q: What diseases is DA-1726 being developed to treat?

MetaVia is targeting five conditions: (1) Obesity — primary weight-loss indication; (2) MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, formerly NAFLD); (3) MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, formerly NASH) — the progressive inflammatory form; (4) MetALD — MASLD with significant alcohol intake; (5) ALD (alcohol-related liver disease). The glucagon receptor agonism is specifically anti-steatotic and makes DA-1726 mechanistically appropriate for liver disease beyond weight loss alone. No effective approved therapy exists for MASLD/MASH as of November 2026 (resmetirom was approved for MASH in 2024 with accelerated approval, but its long-term outcomes data are pending), making this an area of significant unmet need.

Research Limitations

  • DA-1726 is in Phase 1 — the earliest clinical stage; efficacy data require Phase 2/3 confirmation in larger randomized trials
  • Interim results from n=19 participants (15 drug, 4 placebo): sample size is very small and results subject to revision at topline
  • No peer-reviewed publication yet; all data from company press releases and conference presentations
  • GI-related adverse events (nausea, diarrhea) expected during titration — typical for GLP-1/glucagon class; long-term safety not yet established
  • No Phase 2/3 trials registered as of November 2026; topline Phase 1 data Q4 2026 needed to plan next-stage development
  • No regulatory filings anywhere as of November 2026
  • ObesityWeek 2026 poster comparison to retatrutide not yet presented (November 14, 2026)

All efficacy and safety data are from preliminary Phase 1 presentations. No information here constitutes medical advice. Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use. Consult a healthcare provider before any clinical consideration.

meta.description: DA-1726 is MetaVia's oxyntomodulin analog and dual GLP-1R/GCGR agonist showing 68% liver fat reduction and 13.5% weight loss in Phase 1. Research dossier covering mechanism, clinical data, MASLD/MASH indications, and ObesityWeek 2026 presentation.
